boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Belmont record (November 7, 1861) in Operations at the Ohio and Mississippi River Confluence [November 1861]. Oglesby's expedition against Thompson, the Paducah demonstration toward Columbus and the Columbus batteries' fire are context. Campaign-wide marches, returns, reinforcements and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads Division for each side; the live field reads zero. Grant says his expedition amounted to 3,114 men of all arms (on November 5 he expected probably not more than 3,000), and later that Southern sources put the enemy in the field at over 9,000. Pillow says his regiments were each below 500 for duty and numbered about 2,500 all told, that he fought 2,000 men against 7,450, and that he withstood three times his number; on November 12 he gives his division about 2,700 effective after its losses. He puts the Union cavalry at 450.
claims.rationale: Embarked, engaged and after-action figures of different scopes, with each side's estimate of the other and reinforcements from Columbus during the day. None is adopted as a matched opening strength. The live zero is not measured absence.

claims.value: Grant says Belmont lies on low ground commanded by the guns across the river, and that the camp was protected by felled timber forming a sort of abatis. Pillow says a line of felled timber helped defeat the attempt on his left, and that he had no choice of position and no time to reconnoitre.
claims.rationale: Ground and prepared obstacles described by the two opposing commanders; no map verification.

Pillow crossed on Polk's instructions to meet the advancing force.

claims.value: The frozen commanders are Brigadier Generals Gideon J. Pillow and Ulysses S. Grant; the live page gives Grant as Lieutenant General. Pillow crossed under Polk's orders, placed Marks at the head of the flanking column, and says Polk ordered the pursuit continued with the whole force. Grant praises McClernand and says his own horse was shot under him.
claims.rationale: Command roles from the two reports; Polk's part is attributed as Pillow gives it. No automatic sole credit, and the live rank is not adopted.

claims.value: The frozen and live results read Union victory; NPS says the Union force withdrew and re-embarked after the Confederate counterattack. Grant says his troops charged and again defeated the enemy who came between them and the transports; Pillow calls the day glorious to Confederate arms and a victory scarcely paralleled.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 1,464 (US 498; CS 966); the live field reads 1,248 (US 607; CS 641). Grant reports 85 killed, 301 wounded and 99 missing, 175 prisoners taken, and later the enemy's killed and wounded as not less than a figure read 'GOO' in OCR. Pillow's November 9 dispatch gives his loss as about 400; his report transmits a list (not printed) numbering a figure read 'G32', 562 of them in the force first engaged, says 295 Union dead were buried and estimates the Union loss at not less than 2,000; on November 12 he gives his division's loss as 530.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. OCR-garbled figures are retained as printed in the scan.

open_questions: Polk's No. 14 reports, McClernand's, Walke's and the regimental reports on both sides, Brinton's medical report, Pillow's casualty list (not found by the compilers), returns and maps remain deferred. Manning F. Force's From Fort Henry to Corinth (Scribner, 1881) was located (its index lists Belmont at pp.19-21) but not read or selected: the three-family ceiling was taken by the two commanders' reports.

NPS/CWSAC (the live battle page and the frozen Arnold rows) is one family. Grant's November 5, 17 and 20, 1861 reports are one family of interested Union accounts, the same author family as the registered Grant Shiloh report and memoirs (group or-grant); the November 17 report is dated as printed in the OCR. Pillow's November 9, 10 and 12, 1861 reports are one family of interested Confederate accounts. Official Records volumes are shared containers, not additional witnesses. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
